clue.text: Utterly blown out from wordsmith

indicators.note: letters that are blown out are scattered by the wind and land in a new order

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter as the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone is completely exhausted after a bout of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Bulwer-Lytton was the Victorian novelist best remembered for opening a book with 'It was a dark and stormy night'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulwer-Lytton was a prolific Victorian novelist, playwright and politician, so he counts as a professional writer.

clue.text: Eleventh hour in the BBC Book Department?

blocks.note: surface reading: the last possible moment before a deadline
setter's reading: literally eleven at night, the time of a long-running Radio 4 reading slot for books

explanation.surface: A frantic last-minute rush inside the BBC's publishing department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book at Bedtime' is a long-running BBC Radio 4 programme in which a novel is read aloud late in the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven o'clock at night is a typical hour for going to sleep, taking the phrase literally rather than as a deadline idiom.

clue.text: Witch reverting to nameless creature

indicators.note: reverting means going back, so the word is read from its end to its start
without a name means the usual abbreviation for name is dropped

blocks.note: a creature is an animal
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A witch transforms back into a creature with no name.
explanation.walkthrough: The creature is turned round first, then its N is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical myth a lamia is a monstrous woman or sorceress who preys on children, hence a witch.

clue.text: Old forty-niner's right to raise hell

blocks.note: ex means former or old
a gold prospector of 1849 had the right to dig his staked-out claim

explanation.surface: A veteran of the California gold rush is entitled to make trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The forty-niners were the 1849 California gold rush prospectors. To raise 'Hell!' is to shout out a curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Crying out a word such as 'Hell!' is to call out suddenly, so raising that oath is a sudden cry.

clue.text: See 1
Why, some say, a French priest has the right to talk nonsense

indicators.note: what some people say is heard rather than seen, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: the letter Y is pronounced like the word why
an abbé is a French cleric
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a French cleric is entitled to spout rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Yabber is Australian slang for chatter or jabber.
explanation.definitionFit: Yabber is informal Australian slang meaning to chatter or jabber away without much sense.

clue.text: One might own the body of this designer's  work

blocks.clueFragment: One might own the body of this designer's  work
blocks.note: surface reading: a collector owns the whole output of an artist
setter's reading: the work is drawn on someone's skin, so its owner owns the body it is on

explanation.surface: An art collector might possess an entire body of work by one designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who inks designs into skin is an artist whose work is literally carried on the client's body.

clue.text: This paint completely dry, is it?

blocks.clueFragment: This paint completely dry, is it?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone checking whether a fresh coat has dried
setter's reading: a paint formulated so that it does not run or let drops fall from the brush

explanation.surface: A decorator touches a wall and asks if the paint has dried yet.
explanation.definitionFit: Thixotropic paint sold as not running off the brush is described with exactly this hyphenated label on the tin.

clue.text: What 1 across 4 wrote applied to times of ashy destruction

blocks.note: first meaning: the title of the 1834 novel by the author at 1 across
second meaning: literally the final period of the Roman town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79

explanation.surface: A novel's title is applied to a period of fiery ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: Bulwer-Lytton's novel describes the eruption of Vesuvius, and the title also literally describes the town's final moments.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a famous Victorian novel and also literally describes the last period of the Roman town smothered in volcanic ash.

clue.text: Dustman

blocks.note: surface reading: a refuse collector
setter's reading: the man made from the dust of the ground in Genesis

explanation.walkthrough: A dustman is the British word for a bin collector; in Genesis God forms the first man from dust.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible says the first human was formed from dust of the ground, making him literally a man of dust.

clue.text: Consort making name in Co-Conran creation

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the shop's name

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, taken as written
Terence Conran founded the Habitat chain of furniture shops
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A spouse is created by a joint design venture with Terence Conran.
explanation.walkthrough: Habitat is the British home-furnishing store founded by designer Terence Conran in 1964.
explanation.definitionFit: A consort is a companion or partner, and one who shares a home with another lives together with them.

clue.text: Where the ayatollahs lie in state with an omophagous Amazonian

indicators.note: lying in something means sitting inside it, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: PA is the abbreviation for Pennsylvania
the country ruled by ayatollahs since 1979

explanation.surface: Dead religious leaders lie in state beside a raw-flesh-eating creature from the Amazon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie in state' suggests a funeral, but 'lie' just means are located, and the state is American. Pirana is a variant spelling of piranha.
explanation.definitionFit: Omophagous means eating raw flesh, which fits the notorious meat-eating fish of South American rivers.

clue.text: Son of Slad's directors catching my drift with this?

blocks.note: Laurie Lee grew up in the Gloucestershire village of Slad, described in Cider with Rosie
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: A writer's company directors understand what I mean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching my drift' sounds like 'understanding me', but it is literal: a sailing barge's side plank stops it drifting downwind.
explanation.definitionFit: This plank lowered on the side of a sailing vessel resists sideways leeway, so it checks the boat drifting off course.

clue.text: North Atlantic threat a pretext to make an Italian hop

blocks.note: an iceberg, the hazard that sank the Titanic
taken as written
a mask is a cover or pretence

explanation.surface: A shipping danger is used as an excuse for a quick trip to Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hop' suggests a short flight, but it means a dance; the bergamask comes from Bergamo and appears in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: A bergamask is a rustic dance associated with Bergamo in northern Italy, and hop is informal for a dance.

clue.text: Girl wearing underwear here in Texas

blocks.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
in Britain a vest is a sleeveless undershirt
clothes being worn are on

explanation.surface: A young woman is seen in her underwear somewhere in Texas.
explanation.definitionFit: Galveston is a port city on the Gulf coast of the Lone Star State, so it is a place there.

clue.text: "With ____ of leaves and ripple of rain" (Thwinburne)

definitions.text: "With ____ of leaves and ripple of rain"

blocks.clueFragment: "With ____ of leaves and ripple of rain"
blocks.note: surface reading: a missing word in a line from the chorus of Swinburne's Atalanta in Calydon
setter's reading: the poet's name is spelt with th for s, showing the speech defect itself

explanation.surface: A misspelt poet's name is attached to a quoted line of verse about leaves and rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The rustling of leaves is called by this word for soft sibilant speech, and the misspelling acts out the same impediment.

clue.text: The limit of Procol Harum's colour chart?

blocks.note: first meaning: a boundary, as in beyond the ...
second meaning: the shade in the band's 1967 hit A Whiter Shade of ..., placed on a paint chart

explanation.surface: Someone asks about the extent of a rock band's colour range.
explanation.walkthrough: Procol Harum's 1967 hit was 'A Whiter Shade of Pale'; a pale is also a fenced boundary, hence 'beyond the pale'.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a fence or boundary, while the adjective describes a washed-out light colour.

clue.text: See 8
Coming before the water hazard

blocks.note: an advent is an arrival or coming
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A golfer approaches the pond guarding the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water hazard' looks like a golfing term, but the words split: the Ure is a Yorkshire river, and hazard is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, hazard means a risky undertaking or chance, and an exploit with uncertain outcome is exactly that.

clue.text: Levantine gentleman speaking, initially, of France and North Dakota

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the place names that follow
speaking means the letters are pronounced as their spoken names

blocks.note: the opening letter of the country
the initials of the US state
the three letters said out loud as letter names

explanation.surface: A gentleman from the eastern Mediterranean talks about France and an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: Said out loud, the letters F, N, D run together as 'eff-en-dee'.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi was a title of respect for a man of education or standing in Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean.

clue.text: Thus the Colossus managed to carry the first load of bricks

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it within, so the outer word wraps the others

blocks.note: ran means managed, as one runs a business
a hod is the trough a builder carries bricks in, and its contents
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A famous giant statue is said to have hauled a builder's first batch of bricks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant bronze statue, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
explanation.definitionFit: The statue stood on the Aegean island of Rhodes, so it was of that island, and the adjective describes it.

clue.text: Against entering trade disruption at short notice

definitions.note: short indicates the clipped form of advertisement

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the single letter goes within the word for business
disruption throws the letters into disorder so they must be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
v is short for versus, meaning against

explanation.surface: Opposition to a strike causes trade disruption at very little warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short notice' reads as an idiom for little warning, but it means a clipped word for a notice.
explanation.definitionFit: This word is the shortened form of advertisement, which is a public notice promoting something.

clue.text: Ash Wednesday, oddly enough, not so fast

blocks.note: an ember is a glowing piece of ash from a fire
Wednesday is a day of the week

explanation.surface: Someone observes that Ash Wednesday is, surprisingly, not much of a fast.
explanation.walkthrough: Ember days are quarterly church fasts on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays; the setter remarks that Ash Wednesday, oddly, is not one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ember days are days of fasting and prayer observed four times a year in the Western church.

clue.text: Captain Scott names the game hunter

blocks.note: first meaning: the Antarctic explorer's middle name, Robert ... Scott
second meaning: a bird of prey trained to hunt game

explanation.surface: The polar explorer Captain Scott identifies a big-game hunter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Names' looks like a verb, but it means the explorer's names: his full name was Robert Falcon Scott.
explanation.definitionFit: This middle name belonged to the polar explorer, and the bird of prey is flown by falconers to catch game birds.

clue.text: Alternative medicine man

blocks.note: surface reading: a practitioner of homeopathy or herbal remedies
setter's reading: a stand-in doctor, an alternative to the usual one

explanation.surface: A practitioner of complementary therapies.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin-derived word names a doctor who temporarily stands in for another, so a substitute physician.

clue.text: Populate the county? Cool it!

blocks.note: settlers populate new land
County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone told to colonise a county is then told to calm down.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are exclamations telling an excited person to calm themselves and stop making a fuss.

clue.text: Harry Ramsden's contribution to IT?

blocks.note: surface reading: what a famous British seafood restaurant chain serves alongside its battered cod
setter's reading: a small silicon component at the heart of computer hardware

explanation.surface: A fish-and-chip restaurant chain wonders what it has added to computing.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Ramsden's is a British fish-and-chip restaurant chain founded in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a fried potato strip served with fish and a microprocessor in computing.

clue.text: Some coal left out for fire

indicators.note: left out means the letter standing for left is removed

blocks.note: lignite is a soft brown type of coal
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Some coal is put aside to burn later.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to fire something is to set it alight or kindle it.

clue.text: Anthropologist's objective in Melton Mowbray?

blocks.note: surface reading: the human being studied by someone researching humanity
setter's reading: the Leicestershire town famous for pork pies, so its typical man is one who sells them

explanation.surface: A researcher of humankind sets out to study the people of a Leicestershire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire is famous for its pork pies.
explanation.definitionFit: A seller of pastry goods, as in the nursery rhyme about Simple Simon, would be the town's representative human.
